activities.caption: pair each component with its standard test
activities.name: strCompMatch

config.prompt: Distinct adaptations, distinct tests — match them:

pairs.right: one-repetition maximum (1RM) deadlift or squat; handgrip dynamometry
how many press-ups, how long a plank
vertical jumps, broad jumps, medicine-ball throws

config.why: Strength is the foundation of power — you cannot express force quickly that you cannot produce at all — and a good test is valid, reliable and specific to the goal.

activities.anchor: The overload dial has several settings
activities.caption: the bench has stalled — turn a dial
activities.name: strStallBranch

config.root: Your bench press has sat at the same 3 × 5 for three weeks. The stimulus must rise — but which dial do you turn?

start.text: Same weight, same reps, stalled. Pick the overload move:

choices.label: Add load — put a plate on
choices.feedback: The classic move: a heavier stimulus at fewer reps — adaptation restarts.

choices.label: Add reps — turn 3 × 5 into 3 × 6
choices.feedback: More volume at the same load — the 2-for-2 rule's spirit: when you exceed the target, raise the demand.

choices.label: Add density — shorten the rests
choices.feedback: The same work in less time — a different axis of the same principle.

choices.label: Swap the exercise — confuse the muscle
choices.feedback: Muscle confusion dies here: muscles respond to progressive tension, and a new exercise destroys the overload track record you need.

load.text: A rising stimulus — the one non-negotiable principle, satisfied.

reps.text: Volume is sets × reps × load — this satisfies it too.

density.text: The dose rises on the time axis instead of the bar.

confusion.text: No baseline, no progression — variety has real but lesser jobs, and growth is not one of them.

config.why: Load, repetitions, sets and density are the overload dial's settings — everything else is optimisation around the rule that the stimulus keeps rising.

config.text: The first 4–8 weeks of strength are mostly neural: %%0%% — activating more motor units; %%1%% — faster firing for more force per unit; and %%2%% — better sequencing, less co-contraction of antagonists.
config.hint: One is about how many units, one about how fast they fire, one about the pattern itself.

activities.caption: file the growth claims under their signal
activities.name: strGrowthSort

config.prompt: Three signals drive hypertrophy — file each claim:

items.label: the primary signal — high tension per fibre, sustained
the burn and the pump — a secondary contributor at best
effective reps: the repetitions close to failure, where the largest motor units are recruited
growth rises into roughly 10–20 hard sets per muscle group per week

config.why: The classic rep continuum survives as a description of convenience, not biology — light sets of 25–30 to failure and heavy sets of 5 grow comparable muscle when volume is equated.

config.prompt: The strength programme, assembled in order:
items: Build from compound patterns — squat, hinge, press, pull, carry
Put the highest-skill, heaviest work first, while fresh
Fill specific gaps with single-joint accessories afterwards
Rest 2–5 minutes on heavy strength sets; 1–2 on hypertrophy accessories
Train each muscle at least twice a week — the synthesis response stays elevated only 24–48 hours
config.why: Full range of motion as a default — growth is particularly sensitive to loading at long muscle lengths — and power work shifts to velocity with full recoveries.

activities.caption: one habit in this session plan is wrong — click it
activities.name: strWarmupSpot

config.prompt: One line of this session plan is wrong — click it:
lines: Warm up: 5–10 minutes of easy cardio, then the day's first exercise at 40%, 60% and 80% of the working weight.
Right before the heavy sets: 30 seconds of static stretching on the target muscles.
Lift with a neutral spine, hips and legs doing the work rather than the lumbar erectors.
Keep progression in skill ahead of progression in load.
config.correction: Static stretching before lifting measurably reduces force output for minutes — it belongs after training; ramp the loads instead.
config.why: Most gym injuries arrive in the week the lifter got greedy — technique standards are injury prevention with a strength dividend.

activities.caption: true or false — the quantified differences
activities.name: strSexJudge

statements.s: Men carry more muscle mass, and more of it is upper-body.
statements.why: The absolute difference is real; the relative story is different.

statements.s: Relative strength and hypertrophy gains — as a percentage of starting point — are comparable between women and men.
statements.why: Across the literature the percentage gains are comparable, and women's greater fatigue resistance in some protocols does not change programme design.

statements.s: Women will get bulky from lifting.
statements.why: The claim fails on both mechanism (hypertrophy is slow and dose-dependent) and evidence.

activities.caption: the novice vs the lapsed lifter — drag the divider
activities.name: strRegainCompare

config.prompt: Two lifters, same programme — drag the divider:

before.label: the novice
before.text: builds strength slowly — every adaptation, neural and structural, must be created from zero

after.label: the lapsed lifter
after.text: regains strength far faster — retained motor patterns survive, and myonuclei added during growth appear to persist through atrophy

config.why: Maintenance doses — as little as one hard session per muscle per week — hold most of the adaptation until life allows the full programme again.
